Dear Waypoint Mobility Hiring Team,

I'm applying for the Data Scientist, Demand Forecasting role. For the past three years I've worked on transit ridership data, first preparing reports for transit planners and then building forecasting models. I'd like to keep doing that work at Waypoint, where forecasts reach planners in more than 40 cities. I finish my M.S. in Data Science at Lakeshore University in December 2026.

As a research assistant in Lakeshore's Urban Analytics Lab, I built bus ridership forecasting models with XGBoost and LightGBM. They used four years of automatic passenger counter data joined with anonymized third-party mobility data. I led the feature engineering and evaluation, and I'm first author on the resulting UrbanDS 2025 workshop paper. On a 2023 holdout, our model cut MAPE from 14.2% for a SARIMA seasonal baseline to 9.8%. The most useful features were the day of the week, the previous week's boardings, the school calendar, and a mobility index. A reviewer raised possible leakage from the one-week-lagged mobility features, so I re-ran the models with a two-week lag. Error rose to 10.4% but still clearly beat the baseline. That check shaped how I evaluate forecasts: I look for the assumptions that could make a model seem better than it is.

Before graduate school, I was a Data Analyst at Lakeshore Regional Transit Authority. I maintained the Tableau and SQL ridership dashboards used by the planning department. I also automated the weekly reporting pipeline in Python, which cut preparation time from about six hours to one. That job showed me what planners need from a number: it has to arrive on time, and they need to trust where it came from.

I've also learned to explain model results to people who don't build models. As a Data Science Intern at Northpoint Insurance this summer, I raised a churn model's validation AUC from 0.71 to 0.76 using gradient boosting and calibrated its probabilities. I then presented the results to the retention team and a VP, focusing on which customer segments the model flags and how outreach could be prioritized. As a TA for a statistics course for non-majors, I've spent two semesters explaining uncertainty to students who don't come from a technical background.

I haven't deployed a model to production yet. My churn model went to the retention analytics team for further evaluation. Working with engineering to get models into production is something I'm eager to do at Waypoint, and I already have the transit data experience and the habits around forecast evaluation that the role needs.

Thank you for your consideration. I'd welcome the chance to talk.

Sincerely,
Morgan Reyes

# Statement of Purpose: Morgan Reyes
**PhD in Computer Science (Human-Computer Interaction), Khoury College of Computer Sciences, Fall 2027**

As a research assistant working on bus ridership forecasting, I spent part of a summer testing features built from a vendor's mobility data: anonymized device location pings, aggregated to census block groups. One feature I tried combined where frequent riders first boarded with nighttime mobility patterns. It didn't improve the model, so I dropped it, like most features I tested. Before I did, though, I noticed that it concentrated many riders into just a few blocks.

Nothing went wrong. The data was anonymized and aggregated, the feature never left exploratory analysis, and the vendor's documentation said the data came from partner apps with opt-in consent. Still, when I read that documentation, I doubted that anyone tapping "allow" in an app had imagined their location helping to forecast bus ridership, much less being linked to where they boarded a bus. That informal observation has stayed with me longer than any result from the project. It's the main reason I'm applying to study HCI.

## The same gap from the other side

A year later I saw the same gap from the other direction. In a Human-Centered Data Science course, my team of three ran think-aloud usability sessions with five classmates using an AutoML dashboard, and I wrote the findings section of our report. Every participant accepted the tool's top-ranked model without checking its metrics. No one opened the feature-importance panel. Two participants assumed the tool already "knew" which columns in their data were sensitive.

It was a small, unpublished class project, and I don't overstate what it shows. But it showed me that the people who use data systems can misunderstand them in the same way as the people whose data feeds them. In the mobility case, people agreed to data collection they probably couldn't picture. In the AutoML case, users trusted protections the tool didn't offer. In both cases, what people imagined the system was doing differed from what it actually did, and nobody had to act badly for that gap to exist.

## How I got here

My path into this question went through building systems, not studying them. After my B.A. in Economics, I spent a year as a Data Analyst at Lakeshore Regional Transit Authority. I maintained the ridership dashboards used by the planning department and automated our weekly reporting pipeline. That job introduced me to the idea that the numbers I produced would be read and acted on by people who hadn't produced them.

During my M.S. in Data Science, I joined Prof. S. Patel's Urban Analytics Lab. There I built gradient-boosted models to forecast bus ridership recovery from four years of automatic passenger counter data and a mobility index. I led the feature engineering and evaluation and was first author on our UrbanDS 2025 workshop paper. Our model reduced MAPE from 14.2% for a seasonal baseline to 9.8% on a 2023 holdout. When a reviewer raised possible leakage from our lagged mobility features, I re-ran the analysis with a longer lag and reported the higher error, 10.4%, alongside the original. That project taught me how to evaluate carefully and how to report results that are less flattering. It also showed me that the questions I kept coming back to were about people, not model accuracy.

This past summer, as a Data Science Intern at Northpoint Insurance, I built a churn model that raised validation AUC from 0.71 to 0.76, then presented it to the retention team and a VP. I spent much of my preparation figuring out how to explain AUC to a non-technical audience and how to frame the model's outputs as decisions about which customers to contact. I've also been a TA for two semesters in STAT 1100, a statistics course for non-majors, holding weekly office hours and grading final data projects. Both roles gave me practice translating between how analysts think about data and how everyone else encounters it.

## Research interests

My research agenda is still forming, and I expect a PhD to sharpen it. Right now I'm drawn to three related questions:

1. **People's mental models of how their data is used.** When someone consents to data collection through a one-time prompt, what do they picture happening to their data? How far is that from how the data is actually aggregated, combined, and modeled downstream? Could consent interfaces or disclosures close that gap in practice, and not just on paper?
2. **Assumed safeguards in ML tools.** Our AutoML participants assumed protections the tool didn't provide. How common are these assumptions about what ML tools do on users' behalf, and how should tools surface their limits?
3. **Appropriate reliance on model outputs.** When non-experts get predictions or rankings, what leads them to over-rely or under-rely on those outputs? Which interface designs change that?

What connects these questions is the gap between what people believe a data system does and what it actually does, whether those people are the ones whose data the system uses or the ones who rely on its outputs. My background is mostly quantitative, and I see that as useful for this work. I know from experience how data gets joined, aggregated, and turned into features, which helps me ask concrete questions about where people's expectations and actual practice diverge. What I need from a PhD is training in qualitative and mixed methods, study design, and HCI theory, so I can study these gaps rigorously instead of just noticing them.

## Why Khoury

[**To fill in:** name 1–3 Khoury HCI faculty whose work fits the questions above, especially anyone working on privacy, consent, or human-AI interaction. Add a sentence on a specific paper of theirs and how it connects to your interests.]

My questions sit between HCI, privacy, and machine learning, and I want a program where those areas work closely together.

## Looking ahead

I finish my M.S. in December 2026. Long term, I want to do research that shapes how data systems are designed around the people they affect, both the people who use their outputs and the people whose data they are built from. I've spent three years learning how these systems are built. I want to spend the next several years understanding what happens when they meet people who never see how they work.

# Statement of Purpose: Morgan Reyes
**PhD in Computer Science (Human-Computer Interaction), Khoury College of Computer Sciences, Fall 2027**

The mobility data our lab used came from apps on people's phones. According to the vendor's documentation, users had agreed to share it through a one-time opt-in. My first reaction when I read that was: *I doubt anyone tapping "allow" pictured this.*

I was a research assistant at the time, testing features for a bus ridership model. One feature combined where frequent riders first boarded with nighttime mobility patterns. It didn't help the model, so I dropped it. Before I did, I noticed that it concentrated many riders into just a few blocks. Nothing went wrong. The data was anonymized and aggregated, and the feature never went anywhere. But I've thought about that moment more than about anything in the paper we published.

What stayed with me wasn't really a question about data. It was a question about people: what did they think they were agreeing to? Somewhere between an "allow" button and a model's feature set, there's a gap between what a person imagines and what actually happens. I'd spent a long time on the technical side of that gap without ever asking about the other side.

## Seeing it again

In a Human-Centered Data Science course last spring, my team ran think-aloud sessions with five classmates using an AutoML tool. Nearly everything we saw was some form of misplaced trust. Everyone accepted the tool's top-ranked model without looking further. No one opened the explanations. Two participants assumed the tool already knew which columns in their data were sensitive.

That last finding felt familiar. It was the consent prompt again, this time from the user's side: someone trusting a system to be doing something it wasn't. It was a small class project, and I know one usability study is a starting point, not a background. But it was the first time I'd studied this gap directly instead of just noticing it, and I wanted to keep going.

## Where I'm coming from

I came to HCI through data science, and I won't pretend otherwise. I worked as an analyst at a transit agency, built ridership forecasting models as a research assistant, and spent this past summer building a churn model at an insurance company. That work taught me how data actually gets collected, joined, aggregated, and turned into something a model can use. That's why I find the gap between those steps and what people picture so specific and so hard to ignore.

When I try to describe what I want to work on next, I keep landing on the same phrase: something with people and AI, not just building models.

## What I want to study

More concretely, I want to understand what people believe data systems are doing, both with their data and on their behalf, and what happens when those beliefs are wrong. How does someone who tapped "allow" once picture their data being used a year later? Could disclosures or consent designs change that picture in a meaningful way, not just on paper? When people use ML tools, which protections do they assume are built in, and how should tools be honest about what they don't do?

I don't have a full research agenda yet, and I'd rather say that than invent one. What I do have is a set of questions I keep coming back to, technical experience that helps me make those questions concrete, and a real need for the methods I haven't learned yet: interviewing, qualitative analysis, and study design. Those are what I'm hoping to learn at Khoury.

## Why Khoury

## Looking ahead

I finish my M.S. in December 2026. I've spent the last few years on the side of data systems where people are rows in a table. I want to spend the next few years on the side where they're the ones tapping "allow."
